item.title: Diversity of planetary origins and compositions traced by stellar abundance differences of co-natal star systems
item.dc:creator: Bertram Bitsch, Fan Liu, Haiyang S. Wang
item.description: Why It Matters Imagine two siblings raised in the same household who end up with slightly different diets. Astronomers face a similar puzzle with "co-natal" stars: wide pairs of stars born from the same cloud of gas and dust, which should have identical chemical makeup. In a small fraction of these pairs, though, the stars differ in their chemistry. The leading explanation is that one star swallowed a planet, and that planet's material changed the star's outer layers. If that is right, a star's chemistry can reveal what a planet was made of, even after the planet is gone. What They Did The researchers took an existing sample of these paired stars and worked out what kind of planets would have to be swallowed to produce the measured differences. They looked at two groups of elements. Refractory elements (iron, magnesium, silicon) are rocky materials that stay solid even when warm. Volatile elements (oxygen, carbon, sulfur) turn to gas more easily. They compared the pattern of differences in each pair against how planets form at different distances from their star, using "evaporation fronts" as markers. These are the distances where ices such as water, or carbon-bearing grains, change from solid to gas. Key Findings When both refractory and volatile elements are enhanced in one star, a single swallowed planet can explain it. When the rocky elements are enhanced but oxygen and carbon are unchanged or lower, the pattern requires both stars to have swallowed planets that formed in different places, one inside and one outside an evaporation front. Some pairs show sulfur differences several times smaller than those of iron, silicon and magnesium. The authors suggest a planet may have migrated inward across the evaporation front for an iron-sulfur compound (FeS). It would first have collected plenty of sulfur and then none, while still gathering the other rocky elements, before being swallowed. Looking Forward The study suggests that detailed stellar chemistry can serve as a way to measure the composition of exoplanets, planets orbiting other stars. It also points to a wide diversity of planet compositions, which matches what planet formation models predict. The abstract does not give the number of star pairs analyzed.

item.title: Demographics of Close-In TESS Exoplanets Orbiting FGK Main-sequence Stars II. Spectral-Type Dependence and the Neptunian Landscape
item.dc:creator: Kaiming Cui et al.
item.description: Why It Matters Planets don't form in a vacuum: the star they orbit shapes what kind of planets it ends up with. Astronomers want to know whether hotter, more massive stars make different planets than cooler, smaller ones, because that is a clue to how planets are born and how they change over time. Close to a star, there is also a puzzling "Neptunian desert," a region where medium-sized, Neptune-like planets are surprisingly rare. Mapping this empty zone helps test our ideas about how planets form and evolve. What They Did The team used images from NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS), a space telescope that watches stars for tiny dips in brightness when a planet passes in front. They split the stars into three groups, F-type (hotter), G-type (Sun-like), and K-type (cooler), and counted how common planets are on tight orbits of 0.5 to 16 days and sizes of 2 to 20 times Earth's radius. They then modelled the Neptunian desert directly in terms of how often planets occur, and tested statistically whether a distinct "ridge" of Neptune-sized planets stands out. Key Findings Overall, close-in planets are about equally common around all three star types: roughly 12, 10, and 13 per 100 stars for F, G, and K stars. Any differences are therefore local, not global. Hot Jupiters, giant planets on very close orbits, are rarer but peak around K stars, at about 0.67 percent versus 0.50 percent for G and 0.30 percent for F. This is the first such measurement for K stars. The Neptunian desert stretches to longer orbital periods around hotter stars. About one close-in planet in a hundred sits inside the desert, which is roughly twice as populated around K stars as around F stars. A distinct Neptunian ridge is not required to explain the data. Looking Forward These measurements give theorists firm numbers to test planet formation and migration models against. Future work can check whether the desert's shape holds up with more data and better stellar information.

item.title: The ALMA Survey of Gas Evolution of PROtoplanetary disks (AGE-PRO): Evolution of dust properties from multi-wavelength observations
item.dc:creator: Camila Pulgarés et al.
item.description: Why It Matters Planets are born in the flat, spinning clouds of gas and dust around young stars, called protoplanetary discs. The dust is the raw material, a bit like flour and sugar for baking: the cores of giant planets and rocky worlds like Earth are built from it. To understand how planets form, we need to know how much dust a disc holds, how warm it is, and how big its grains grow, and how all of this changes as the disc ages. What They Did The AGE-PRO project (the ALMA Survey of Gas Evolution of PROtoplanetary disks) used the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), a network of radio telescopes in Chile, to study 30 discs at three life stages: embedded (0.5-1 million years old), middle-age (1-3 million years) and end of life (2-6 million years). Earlier work relied on a single wavelength, 1.3 millimetres. Here the team added new observations at 3.1 and 1.5 millimetres. Looking at several wavelengths is like examining an object under different colours of light: it helps separate how much dust there is from how it absorbs and emits light. They fitted the data and built brightness profiles showing how the glow changes with distance from the star. They resolved 20 of the 30 discs at both new wavelengths, then modelled all the wavelengths together. Key Findings The earlier trends held up. Dust discs stay about the same size as they age, while their dust mass declines. The exact mass is uncertain by a factor of 10-40, depending on assumptions about how the dust grains absorb light. This implies the ratio of gas to dust in these discs is much lower than earlier studies reported. The colour pattern of the glow, called the spectral index, suggests many discs, especially those in the Ophiuchus and Lupus star-forming regions, are optically thick. This means the dust is so dense that it hides material behind it, so we may be underestimating how much is there. Looking Forward The results show that estimates of disc mass depend heavily on the assumptions made about dust, so better dust models are needed. Resolving the discs more finely should clarify how much solid material is really available to build planets.

item.title: ExoVetter and a TESS Exoplanet Transit Search of Kepler Stars as Ground Truth
item.dc:creator: Matthew M. Dallas et al.
item.description: Why It Matters Space telescopes such as the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) watch hundreds of thousands of stars for tiny, regular dips in brightness. These dips can mean a planet is passing in front of its star. But many dips are impostors, such as pairs of stars eclipsing each other, or instrument glitches. Sorting real planet signals from false alarms is like picking out a real coin from a pile of lookalikes, and doing it by hand does not scale to this much data. What They Did The authors built an open-source Python tool called exoVetter. It calculates a set of checks (called vetting metrics) and makes visualizations that help judge whether a dip in starlight is a real planet signal. It is modular and not tied to any one mission, so other teams can adapt it to different telescopes and science goals. To test it, they ran a search for repeating dips, using a method called box-least squares, on 324,530 TESS light curves (records of a star's brightness over time). They limited the search to stars also watched by the Kepler telescope, which is more sensitive. Kepler's results served as "ground truth," a trusted answer key for checking which TESS events were real. Key Findings Using that answer key, the team set baseline thresholds for exoVetter's metrics on TESS data: several based on the star's brightness measurements and one based on whether the dip's apparent position shifts, which can reveal a signal coming from a neighboring star. They also found that for short-period events (planets that orbit quickly), a catalog built from dim stars (fainter than 13.5 in TESS magnitude) could have a similar share of real events to one built from bright stars. Looking Forward These thresholds give other researchers a starting point for sifting through TESS data. The results also suggest that faint stars, often overlooked, could be searched for planets without drowning the catalog in false alarms. That would greatly widen the pool of stars available for planet hunting.

item.title: A Study of the 30 May 2026 Meteor Event Employing Data from Raspberry Boom Infrasound Sensors in the Boston Area
item.dc:creator: S. Africk, A. Loeb
item.description: Why It Matters Every day, space rocks plunge into Earth's atmosphere. The brightest ones, called fireballs, end in a powerful blast. Some of that energy arrives as infrasound, sound pitched too low for human ears. On 30 May 2026, a meteor over Cape Cod Bay produced one of these signals. This study shows that a network of ground sensors, including privately owned ones, can pick up such a signal and work out what happened high overhead. What They Did The researchers gathered recordings from several university and private Raspberry Boom infrasound sensors around the Greater Boston area. Each sensor caught the same faint pressure pulse: about one and a half cycles of a 0.4 hertz wave, a slow swell and dip repeating roughly every two and a half seconds. The team compared arrival times at the different sensors, much as you might guess where thunder came from by noticing which friend heard it first. That gave them the direction to the source. They then examined how arrival time related to each sensor's distance from the event, which let them work out what kind of event it was and where it happened. Finally, they used the strength of the pressure change at each site to estimate how much acoustic power the event released. Key Findings Timing differences between sensors were enough to define the direction to the source. The distance-and-timing analysis identified the signal as the atmospheric blast of the fireball, at an altitude between 40 and 50 kilometers. The pressure measurements indicate that the sound carried roughly 5% to 14% of the fireball's total energy. Looking Forward The results show that modest, widely spread sensors can locate a meteor blast and estimate how much energy it released as sound. Adding more sensors, including privately run ones, could help scientists study future fireballs in the same way.
